justification: The original evidence still supports attributing accountable decision-making to the process in a limited sense: the documented procedure assigns the final case-level decision to the claims reviewer, the reviewer records evidence consulted and a free-text rationale, and disagreements can be escalated to a Senior Claims Reviewer. However, the additional audit information materially weakens the attribution because reviewer performance assessments include an agreement-rate indicator comparing final decisions with model recommendations, and an override rate above 12% triggers managerial review of the reviewer’s case history. Interview evidence that 17 of 21 reviewers considered the agreement-rate indicator when deciding whether to override a recommendation shows that the model agreement metric is influencing reviewer behaviour. This creates a stronger basis for saying the process is not purely attributable to the human final decision-maker alone, even though the human reviewer still formally holds the final disposition. The evidence therefore supports accountable decision-making only partially rather than straightforwardly.
evidence_affected: The documented procedure assigns the final case-level decision to the claims reviewer.
Reviewers enter a free-text rationale when finalising a disposition.
Disagreements between the model recommendation and the reviewer are routed to an organisational role identified as Senior Claims Reviewer.
An internal audit found that reviewer performance assessments include an agreement-rate indicator comparing final decisions with model recommendations.
An override rate above 12% triggers managerial review of the reviewer's case history.
In interviews during the audit, 17 of 21 reviewers reported considering the agreement-rate indicator when deciding whether to override a recommendation.
